name: Wrike
subcategory: team projects, issues and delivery planning
tagline: Track projects through tasks, boards, custom fields, and team dashboards

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Essential task and project management; the current public page does not disclose numeric user, storage or task caps
tiers.notes: A permanent Free plan is listed, but its numeric ceilings were not exposed.

tiers.name: Team
tiers.notes: Displayed per-user monthly equivalent is billed annually.

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: 5–200 users, advanced resource planning/reporting and part of Wrike AI Elite
tiers.notes: Displayed per-user monthly equivalent is billed annually.

tiers.name: Pinnacle
tiers.limits: Custom plan with advanced analytics/resource management and 3× more AI actions than Business

tiers.name: Apex
tiers.limits: Custom plan with 10× more AI actions, unlimited whiteboards and Wrike Integrate/Sync

pricing.freeTierCaps: Free plan exists, but the live public page does not expose numeric user, storage or task caps
pricing.billingTerms: Free + annual-billed paid plans; Business and above annual only; 14-day trial, no card
pricing.hiddenCosts: Seats are sold in bundles: up to 30 in groups of 5, 30–100 in groups of 10 and above 100 in groups of 25. Whiteboard is $15/user/month; Integrate, Sync, Datahub, Lock and AI-action packs are separately quoted. Taxes are extra, and guided deployment is required for 20+ users.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Wrike, track projects through tasks, boards, custom fields, and team dashboards. The hard boundary is enterprise workflow, approvals, integrations, reporting, and governance, plus collaboration, integrations, and organizational trust.
coreLoopDIY: Plan and track projects for a small team through tasks, boards, milestones, custom fields, comments, dashboards, and a searchable activity history.
whatYouLose: enterprise workflow, approvals, integrations, reporting, and governance
ongoingBurden: auth, permissions, notifications, search, migrations, audit history, integrations, backups, and uptime
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Wrike because teams pay because project state has to remain authoritative through staff changes, outages, and years of accumulated workflow exceptions. The recurring cost buys auth, permissions, notifications, search, migrations, audit history, integrations, backups, and uptime, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Plane
priorArt.desc: Active open-source project and issue tracking platform.

alternatives.name: Plane
alternatives.desc: Linear-and-Jira-shaped work tracking without the subscription; the stack behind it is not small

facts.install: Hosted signup, or the official Docker/Kubernetes self-hosting stack
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted Plane keeps workspaces, projects, work items, users, comments, and settings in PostgreSQL; attachments, images, and exports live in MinIO or another S3-compatible object store, with RabbitMQ and optional OpenSearch alongside them. Plane Cloud stores the equivalent data in Plane's infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: Plane lacks Wrike's request forms, proofing and approvals, resource planning, portfolio dashboards, and deep custom reporting for non-engineering work.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting is a multi-service deployment: Docker or Kubernetes plus PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, object storage, a domain, TLS, and usually email configuration.

alternatives.name: OpenProject
alternatives.desc: The enterprise project suite; free in money, expensive in menus

facts.install: Hosted Enterprise Cloud signup, or Community Edition via Docker Compose/all-in-one Docker or supported Linux packages
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted application data lives in PostgreSQL; uploaded attachments live on a persistent filesystem volume or configured S3-compatible object storage, while configuration and any linked repositories must be backed up separately. Cloud data lives in OpenProject's hosted infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: OpenProject is capable but does not match Wrike's polished creative proofing, workload views, no-code automation, and large integration catalog.
facts.setupBlocker: The free Community Edition needs a Linux server; the recommended Docker setup still requires persistent database/file volumes, a hostname, TLS, and mail configuration.

alternatives.name: YouTrack
alternatives.desc: A full project tracker for ten people; user eleven is where JetBrains remembers billing

facts.install: Hosted YouTrack Cloud signup, or the official Docker image for YouTrack Server
facts.dataFormat: YouTrack Server stores issues, users, projects, and configuration in its own integrated on-disk database under the data directory, with separate configuration, logs, and backups directories; YouTrack Cloud keeps the data in JetBrains-managed infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: YouTrack's free ten-user ceiling and developer-first workflow leave Wrike's proofing, request intake, resource allocation, and executive dashboards largely uncovered.
facts.setupBlocker: The cloud edition installs cleanly; self-hosting requires Docker volume mapping, enough storage, a one-time setup token, and external HTTPS/reverse-proxy work for a public server.

alternatives.name: Leantime
alternatives.desc: A small-team project suite that remembers goals and timesheets, not just tickets

facts.install: Paid hosted signup, or the free open-source edition via Docker Compose/official image or a PHP release archive plus MySQL/MariaDB
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted project data lives in MySQL 8 or MariaDB 10.6+, while uploaded files use the local filesystem or configured S3-compatible storage; hosted-account data lives in Leantime's cloud.
facts.gapVsPaid: Leantime has less flexible request intake, custom-field reporting, automation, proofing, and resource management than Wrike.
facts.setupBlocker: There is no longer a permanent free hosted tier: the free route means operating PHP, MySQL/MariaDB, persistent storage, backups, and a web-facing Docker or LAMP stack.

alternatives.name: Redmine
alternatives.desc: Project tracking, time sheets, Gantt, and wikis from the era when software admitted it needed configuration

facts.install: Install the Ruby on Rails application against PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, or SQLite; packaged containers/appliances are third-party conveniences
facts.dataFormat: Issues, users, projects, time entries, and configuration live in the configured SQL database; uploaded attachments live as files in Redmine's `files` directory.
facts.gapVsPaid: Redmine can be customized with plugins, but its dated interface and manual administration are a major step down from Wrike's managed dashboards, proofing, and automations.
facts.setupBlocker: The official install is a real Rails deployment, Ruby and gem versions, database creation, migrations, a production web server, email, backups, and upgrades are all the operator's job.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Team plan and a small-team tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Wrike in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: plan and track projects for a small team through tasks, boards, milestones, custom fields, comments, dashboards, and a searchable activity history.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement organizations, projects, members, issues, labels, cycles, and milestones.
Provide list, kanban, and simple timeline views backed by one canonical issue model.
Add comments, mentions, assignments, watchers, and a complete activity log.
Implement project roles for owner, member, and viewer and test every mutation.
Add search, CSV import or export, email notifications, and daily database backups.
Ship Docker Compose, health checks, migrations, seed data, and an admin recovery command.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out hundreds of external integrations.
Deliberately leave out enterprise portfolio planning and SSO.
Deliberately leave out native mobile clients and vendor-operated uptime.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
